title: Bits & Math Journey
description: Digits, carries, overflow, Euclid's algorithm, primality, sieves, bit masks, and exponentiation.

prerequisites: Array indexing and basic binary notation
journey.outcome: Use numeric representations and invariants safely, including zero, overflow, fixed bit widths, and integer-versus-floating arithmetic.

connections.count-all-digits-of-a-number: Start with repeated division to expose a number's representation. Zero is itself a one-digit number, so it needs attention before a loop that only runs on positive values.
connections.plus-one: Represent a number as digit positions and propagate a carry. The all-nines case changes the representation's length rather than fitting into the existing final position.
connections.reverse-integer: Use remainder extraction and repeated multiplication to build a reversed value. Check representable bounds before multiplying or adding instead of relying on overflow behavior.
connections.multiply-strings: Generalize carries from adding one to combining every digit pair. A digit's output position is determined by both input indices, so accumulation and carry normalization must stay consistent.
connections.gcd-of-two-numbers: Use a remainder invariant to shrink a problem without changing its answer. Euclid's algorithm replaces divisor enumeration with repeated reduction of the larger argument.
connections.codechef-prb01: A composite number has a divisor pair with one member no greater than its square root. This bounds trial division and separates primality from simply checking a few small factors.
connections.count-primes: Move from testing one number to testing a whole range. A sieve shares work by marking multiples of each newly discovered prime instead of repeating trial division for every candidate.
connections.happy-number: Repeated digit processing creates a deterministic state transition. A visited set or fast/slow pointers can detect whether the sequence reaches one or enters another cycle.
connections.sqrtx: Search the final integer whose square is within the input. Division-based comparisons can avoid multiplication overflow when the candidate range is large.
connections.powx-n: Exploit the binary structure of an exponent to halve the work repeatedly. Negative exponents and the most negative integer require care when taking reciprocals and absolute values.
connections.number-of-1-bits: Move from decimal digits to binary positions. Clearing the lowest set bit removes one contribution at a time without scanning every possible position.
connections.single-number: Use XOR cancellation to remove paired occurrences. The result is valid because the input guarantees every other value appears exactly twice, not because XOR finds arbitrary odd-frequency values by itself.
connections.missing-number: Apply cancellation to two related collections: expected indices and observed values. The unmatched expected value remains, with no risk of overflowing an arithmetic total.
connections.counting-bits: Reuse smaller binary states instead of counting each number independently. Removing the lowest set bit links a value to an already solved value with one fewer set bit.
connections.reverse-bits: Treat the input as a fixed-width bit pattern, including leading zeroes. Numeric digit reversal and bit reversal have different stopping conditions.
connections.sum-of-two-integers: Separate addition into sum-without-carry and carry bits. Repeat until no carry remains, using a fixed-width mask where the language has unbounded signed integers.
connections.bitwise-and-of-numbers-range: Across a consecutive range, low bits eventually vary and disappear under AND. Find the shared high-bit prefix instead of evaluating every integer in the interval.
